'''Norman Neill Greenwood''' (19 January 1925 – 14 November 2012<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.leeds.ac.uk/forstaff/news/article/3582/emeritus_professor_norman_greenwood |title=University of Leeds, Obituary notice |access-date=15 February 2022 |archive-date=9 May 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200509140432/https://www.leeds.ac.uk/forstaff/news/article/3582/emeritus_professor_norman_greenwood |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|first=Peter |last=Perkins |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/nov/27/norman-greenwood |title=Norman Greenwood &#124; guardian.co.uk |work=The Guardian|date= 27 November 2012|access-date=2012-11-27 |location=London}}</ref><ref>[https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/norman-greenwood-lshcqkpjpx6 Obituary notice, The Times, 30 November 2012]</ref>) was an Australian-British [[chemist]] and Emeritus Professor at the [[University of Leeds]].<ref name=webofstories>{{cite web | url=https://www.webofstories.com/people/norman.greenwood | title=Norman Greenwood tells his life story (May 2011) | publisher=[[Web of Stories]] | date=25 November 2011 | access-date=2012-07-30 | last=Johnson|first= Brian}}</ref> Together with Alan Earnshaw, he wrote the textbook ''Chemistry of the Elements'', first published in 1984.

==Early life and education==
After attending [[University High School, Melbourne]] (1939–42), Greenwood read [[Chemistry]] at the [[University of Melbourne]] and graduated with a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] in 1945 and an [[Master of Science|MSc]] in 1948. In 1948, he was awarded the Exhibition of 1851 Scholarship to enable him to read for a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] at [[Sidney Sussex College, Cambridge]] under the supervision of [[Harry Julius Emeléus]]. He received the PhD in 1951.<ref name=":4">[https://www.leeds.ac.uk/secretariat/obituaries/2012/greenwood_norman.html University of Leeds, Obituary]</ref>

==Academic career==
Greenwood was a senior research fellow at the [[Atomic Energy Research Establishment]] from 1951 until 1953 when he was appointed a [[lecturer]] at the [[University of Nottingham]].  His first PhD student at [[University of Nottingham|Nottingham]] was [[Kenneth Wade]] (1954–1957).<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.scs.illinois.edu/~mainzv/Web_Genealogy/Info/emeleushj.pdf| title=Harry Julius Emeleus (1903–1993) | work=Chemical Genealogy Database | publisher=[[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] | first= Kenneth |last=Wade| date=21 May 2009 | access-date=2012-07-31}}</ref>

Professor [[William Wynne-Jones, Baron Wynne-Jones|William Wynne-Jones]], who was the Chairman of the School of Chemistry at Kings College, Durham (which was to become the [[Newcastle University|University of Newcastle upon Tyne]] in 1963), recruited Greenwood to the first established chair of inorganic chemistry in the country in 1961.

Greenwood was appointed [[Professor]] and Head of the Department of Inorganic and Structural Chemistry at the [[University of Leeds]] in 1971, a post which he held until his retirement in 1990 when he was given the title [[Emeritus]] Professor.

His researches in inorganic and structural chemistry have made major advances in the chemistry of [[boron hydrides]] and other [[main-group element]] compounds.  He also pioneered the application of [[Mössbauer spectroscopy]] to problems in chemistry.  He was a prolific writer and inspirational lecturer on chemical and educational themes, and has held numerous visiting professorships throughout the world. He was appointed by [[NASA]] as principal investigator in the study of [[lunar rocks]].<ref name=webofstories/> He served as chairman of the IUPAC [[Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights|Commission on Atomic Weights]] from 1970 to 1975 and also as president of the [[IUPAC Inorganic Chemistry Division]].<ref name=":4" />

==Honours==
Greenwood was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 1987.<ref>[https://royalsociety.org/uploadedFiles/Royal_Society_Content/about-us/fellowship/Fellows1660-2007.pdf Royal Society, List of Fellows]</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Johnson|first1=Brian F. G.|last2=Welch|first2=Alan J.|last3=Woollins|first3=J. Derek|last4=Johnson|first4=Charles|last5=Housecroft|first5=Catherine E.|title=Norman Neill Greenwood. 19 January 1925—14 November 2012|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|year=2020|volume=68|pages=195–218|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2019.0015|s2cid=209387095|doi-access=free}}</ref>
